name: Carpal tunnel syndrome

diagnosisContested.note: The condition itself is widely accepted. What is debated is how to diagnose and grade it. A consensus paper found no perfect gold standard and judged electrodiagnostic findings plus symptoms most accurate (rempel_1998). The AAOS/ASSH 2024 guideline says the CTS-6 can be used in lieu of routine ultrasound or nerve testing (shapiro_2025), while an expert consensus says electrodiagnosis should always be performed to quantify severity and in people over 70 (pelosi_2022). Twelve severity grading systems exist and 27% of surveyed practitioners used none (robinson_2026). A secondary summary also reports normal electrodiagnostic results in some symptomatic people (physiotutors_dx_2026), and a Lancet Neurology review reports a paucity of evidence on the best approaches to assessment (padua_2016). Users of this app may be self-identified rather than diagnosed, and the severity limits most non-surgical recommendations rely on cannot be checked from self-report.

avoidOrModify.movement: Sustained or loaded positions near end-range wrist extension or flexion, for example flat-palm push-ups, planks and front-rack holds. These examples are an inference; no study found measured them.
avoidOrModify.rationale: Catheter studies show carpal canal pressure is lowest near neutral and rises with wrist flexion and extension, and more so in people with CTS (mean 32 mmHg neutral, 94 at 90 degrees flexion, 110 at 90 degrees extension, against 2.5, 31 and 30 in controls). In healthy people, 30 mmHg was reached at 32.7 degrees extension (95% CI 27.2-38.1) and 48.6 degrees flexion (37.7-59.4) at the 25th percentile. In 5 cadaveric hands, pressure rose beyond 20 degrees and exceeded 5 times baseline at 50 degrees. Straight fingers gave higher pressure than 45 degrees of knuckle flexion across extension angles, which by inference makes the flat-palm shape a high-pressure posture, though that study was unloaded. Direct support for acting on this is weak: wrist posture was significantly associated under the broader NIOSH case definition but not under a strict nerve-conduction-backed definition (OR 4.73, 95% CI 0.42-53.32), workplace evidence is low quality, and in 21 patients ergonomic devices changed wrist position without lowering pressure. Using a smaller range or a straighter wrist is a reasonable inference, not a tested exercise intervention.

avoidOrModify.movement: High-volume hand work that combines forceful gripping with many repetitions
avoidOrModify.rationale: Occupational studies rate repetition and force as the best-supported risk factors: repetition HR 1.87 (95% CI 1.42-2.46) and force intensity HR 1.84 (1.22-2.79) in prospective cohorts; repetition OR 2.26 (1.73-2.94) and hand force OR 4.23 (1.53-11.68) with nerve-conduction-backed cases. A separate cohort review also supports repetition, velocity and combined exposures. These are years of workplace exposure and may not transfer to gym training. The nearest sport data disagree: 33.3% definite CTS in 27 elite female tug-of-war athletes analysed (the abstract says 29 recruited) with no concurrent control, against no association between training load and CTS in wheelchair athletes. They support managing hand volume, not avoiding hand use. A secondary summary of the 2026 guideline favours individual activity modification over indiscriminate avoidance.

avoidOrModify.movement: Hard or sustained pinching and fingertip loading, and by inference pinch-grip carries and fingertip-heavy holds
avoidOrModify.rationale: In healthy volunteers, small fingertip loads raised carpal tunnel pressure at every wrist angle tested, and pinching produced nearly twice the pressure of pressing at the same force (14.2, 29.9, 41.9 and 49.7 mmHg at 0, 5, 10 and 15 N, against 7.8, 14.1, 20.0 and 33.8). Pinch pressure was at least 18% above power grip or no grip during resisted wrist motion. Epidemiological support is weaker: pooled pinch gripping was not significant (HR 1.84, 95% CI 0.96-3.52). No study found measured hanging or barbell gripping.

avoidOrModify.movement: Hand-transmitted vibration, for example vibrating tools or vibrating grips
avoidOrModify.rationale: Evidence is mixed: odds ratios of 5.40 (95% CI 3.14-9.31) and 2.9 (low risk-of-bias analysis) and a more than 2-fold risk with prolonged tool use, while a later meta-analysis of prospective cohorts found no significant association (HR 1.47, 95% CI 0.63-3.42, I-squared 90%). An overview rated it moderate quality as a risk factor. NHS advice is to cut back on vibrating tools. All of this is occupational; nothing found tested gym vibration platforms or similar.

avoidOrModify.movement: Strong nerve tensioning: holding the wrist, fingers and arm in a position that lengthens the whole median nerve path at once
avoidOrModify.rationale: In cadavers, tensioning techniques strained the median nerve at the wrist far more than sliding techniques (6.8% versus 0.8%). In 15 asymptomatic volunteers, sliding produced far more excursion than tensioning (10.2 versus 1.8 mm, measured in the upper arm). One trial chose sliding to avoid irritating an already compressed nerve, and adjusted speed and amplitude so that movement produced no pain. No clinical trial found shows tensioning causes harm, and therapist-delivered trials have used both techniques, so this is cautious reasoning from mechanics.

avoidOrModify.movement: Hard active gripping or pinching with the wrist bent back, by inference any gripped load held in extension
avoidOrModify.rationale: In 14 healthy adults, resisted wrist motion without gripping changed pressure little, while active pinch or power grip raised it, especially in extension (extension and flexion means: no grip 6.9, power 9.7, pinch 9.8 mmHg; rest 3.5). Loads were 2 N·m or less, far below gym loads. Calculated excursions, not direct measurement, suggest flexor muscle bellies can enter the tunnel in wrist extension, and those cadaver authors advise avoiding flexor use with wrist and fingers extended. A separate cadaver study found contact force on the nerve highest with the wrist flexed under flexor load, so the direction of risk between flexion and extension is not settled. Catheter studies found the lowest pressure near neutral.

avoidOrModify.movement: After carpal tunnel release only: repeated hand and wrist loading, lifting over 10 kg, and hand-held vibrating tools, during the early recovery window
avoidOrModify.rationale: A UK Delphi panel of 33 surgeons and hand therapists gave expected return times: repetitive gripping and releasing 14-28 days; unpredictable hand or wrist contact 14-35 days; repeated loading including sports training 14-35 days; hand-held vibrating tools 21-42 days; lifting or stabilising over 10 kg 21-42 days. The panel agreed that patients should regularly move fingers, thumb and wrist (97%). AAOS/ASSH 2024 advises against routine immobilization and routine supervised therapy after release (Moderate). This is expert consensus, and timescales may lengthen with complications; follow the surgeon's instructions where they differ.

candidateExercises.name: Tendon gliding sequence (finger positions from straight to fist)

dose.frequency: 3 times per week for 3 weeks, used alongside manual therapy (Sheereen 2022). Bartkowiak 2019 used the same 5 repeats and 7-second holds 3 times daily for 2 weeks, without stating sets.

candidateExercises.cautions: These doses come from trials where gliding was combined with other treatment, so they are not proven standalone doses. Sheereen had no control group. Adding gliding to a splint gave no between-group benefit on symptoms in Abdolrazaghi 2023 and Sim 2019, and no between-group difference on BCTQ in Arman 2024. Stop if numbness or tingling increases. Evidence for isolated tendon gliding is reported as less conclusive. The full-fist position draws lumbrical muscle into the tunnel in healthy hands (79.4% of fingers); no outcome data link this to symptoms.

alternativeDoses.frequency: 3 sessions per day for 6 weeks, with a splint. Gave no added benefit over splint alone in mild CTS.
Twice daily at home for 8 weeks with a night splint, 15 seconds rest between series, then at least once daily to week 16. Five tendon positions.
Twice daily plus supervised physiotherapy 3 days per week. Hold and sets not reported.

candidateExercises.name: Median nerve gliding sequence

dose.frequency: Twice daily at home for 8 weeks with a night splint, 15 seconds rest between series, then at least once daily to week 16 (Arman 2024). Six positions. No load or difficulty progression was described.

candidateExercises.cautions: Lowest-confidence candidate. Reviews disagree: Cochrane found very low-quality evidence, Paraskevopoulos 2023 concluded no clinical benefit, Núñez de Arenas-Arroyo 2021 found small short-term effects at very low certainty, and Zaheer 2023 reports clear benefit from trials it describes as physiotherapist-delivered, with no GRADE rating. AAOS/ASSH 2024 says exercise does not improve long-term outcomes (Limited), and the 2019 and 2026 guideline summaries report conflicting evidence with no clear recommendation. In Arman 2024 BCTQ improved in all arms with no between-group difference, and every arm wore a night splint. The sequence includes wrist-extended positions, which raise canal pressure. Keep it gentle, adjust speed and range so it does not produce pain, and stop if symptoms increase. Avoid overstretching the thumb in the final step, which one cross-sectional study says may be omitted; no outcome data test this. Not suitable for anyone with a red flag sign.

alternativeDoses.frequency: 3 times daily for 2 weeks, alongside ultrasound or laser. Sets are our reading; the trial does not state them. This was the earlier primary dose in this file.
3 sessions per day for 6 weeks, with a splint. No added benefit over splint alone.
Daily, in pregnancy. No untreated comparator, so this is not efficacy evidence.

candidateExercises.name: Wrist flexor and extensor stretch, arm straight, using the other hand

dose.frequency: CSP gives 15-30 seconds per stretch, with exercises used for at least 6-8 weeks. Sessions per day or week are not stated. holdSeconds is the upper value.

candidateExercises.cautions: The dose is patient-information advice, not trial data. Guideline support (Grade C) is for stretching combined with an orthosis in mild to moderate CTS without thenar atrophy and with normal two-point discrimination; the specific stretches could not be checked. End-range wrist positions raise canal pressure, so use light pressure and release if tingling starts.

alternativeDoses.frequency: Self-carpal-ligament stretch 4 times per day for 6 weeks. Between-group result inconclusive; only 36 of 83 completed. Not the same stretch.

Lumbrical or general stretches 6 times per day with an orthosis during sleep (Baker trial, as described in the 2019 guideline's public-comment draft marked 'Do Not Cite'). No hold reported in the passage read. No arm was superior; 25.5% progressed to surgery at 24 weeks.

candidateExercises.name: Active wrist bend forward and back, elbow on a table

dose.frequency: Use for at least 6-8 weeks. Sessions per day or week are not stated.

candidateExercises.cautions: CSP describes bending to a right angle, but pressure data show the highest canal pressures at 90 degrees, and a cadaver study found pressure rising beyond 20 degrees. Consider a smaller symptom-free range; that adjustment is our inference and has not been tested.

candidateExercises.name: Finger bend at the middle joints

dose.frequency: Use for at least 6-8 weeks. Sessions per day or week are not stated.

candidateExercises.cautions: Patient-information dose, not trial data. Stop if numbness or tingling increases.

candidateExercises.name: Light palm-down wrist extension with a small weight

dose.frequency: Use for at least 6-8 weeks. Sessions per day or week are not stated.

candidateExercises.cautions: CSP's example load is a tin of beans, far below normal training weight, and the catalog's normal programming should not be assumed to apply. CSP also says to increase the weight gradually, without giving a limit. CSP calls this a stretch, but it is loaded wrist extension. In healthy wrists, resisted motion up to 2 N·m without gripping changed pressure little, but active power grip raised it, especially in extension, and holding a dumbbell needs a grip. No trial found tested this for unoperated CTS. The only resistance trial found was a crossover with one session per condition of elastic-band wrist work to failure at Borg 3 in 22 people at least 3 weeks after release: pain fell, but it shows neither training safety nor benefit, so it is not used as a dose.

candidateExercises.name: Rubber ball hand squeeze

dose.frequency: Use for at least 6-8 weeks. Sessions per day or week are not stated.

candidateExercises.cautions: CSP recommends this, but the pressure data point the other way. Fingertip loading raises canal pressure in healthy volunteers, active power grip raised it during wrist motion, and a full fist draws lumbrical muscle into the tunnel. Squeezing a ball itself was not measured. Use a soft ball and low effort, keep the wrist neutral, and skip it if symptoms increase. Not tested in a trial found.

redFlags.sign: Sudden, rapidly worsening pain and altered sensation in the thumb-side fingers, especially after a wrist fracture, bleeding or a high-pressure injury
redFlags.action: Stop exercise and seek emergency care the same day. Acute carpal tunnel syndrome can need urgent surgical decompression to prevent permanent nerve injury.

redFlags.sign: Hand or thumb weakness, or visible wasting of the muscle at the base of the thumb
redFlags.action: Stop hand and wrist exercises for this condition and get prompt medical assessment. Do not wait for it to pass.

redFlags.sign: Constant numbness or progressive loss of sensation
redFlags.action: Get prompt medical assessment, as this can signal severe nerve injury. Do not rely on exercise.

redFlags.sign: Hand symptoms affecting several nerve areas, or with neck pain, a change in walking or brisk reflexes
redFlags.action: Stop the programme until assessed and get medical evaluation, since this can point to a cervical spinal cord or nerve root problem, other neurological disease or generalised neuropathy rather than carpal tunnel syndrome. A UK commissioning guide lists neurological disease and cervical nerve root entrapment for urgent referral, within 2 weeks.

redFlags.sign: Symptoms getting worse or not going away, daily symptoms with frequent night waking, or functional problems not responding to up to 12 weeks of home or non-surgical treatment
redFlags.action: See a GP or clinician. A UK commissioning guide says outcomes of surgery may be poorer after long periods of persistent symptoms.

redFlags.sign: Tingling or numbness that began after an injury, or a suspected fracture or tumour
redFlags.action: Stop hand and wrist exercise and get medical assessment. The guide lists these as red flags; the passage read gives no time frame, and the same-day rule above applies if symptoms are rapidly worsening.

redFlags.sign: Hand symptoms with active inflammatory joint disease such as gout or rheumatoid arthritis, or with poor circulation to the limb (peripheral limb ischaemia)
redFlags.action: Stop these exercises and seek urgent medical referral. The guide lists these for urgent referral, within 2 weeks.

limitations: Grade stays very_low. The closest evidence on exercise itself is the 2012 Cochrane review (limited, very low quality, 16 studies not pooled, only two measured adverse effects) and later GRADE-rated neurodynamic reviews at low to very low certainty; AAOS/ASSH 2024 rates exercise as not improving long-term outcomes at Limited strength, which is not evidence of harm or of no short-term benefit. Cochrane search ended January 2012. Contradictions. (1) Neurodynamic work: Zaheer 2023 and Jiménez-Del-Barrio 2022 (manual therapy, soft-tissue as well as neurodynamic) report large benefits (BCTQ SSS MD -1.20; SMD -1.67) and Paraskevopoulos 2023 concludes no clinical benefit from statistically positive pooled data; Núñez de Arenas-Arroyo 2021 finds small short-term effects. Pooled effects lean on no-treatment-controlled, therapist-delivered trials such as Wolny 2019, with pain I-squared 96% in Jiménez-Del-Barrio. Cavalcante 2022 rates over 76% of CTS treatment reviews low or very low on AMSTAR. (2) Add-on gliding: Abdolrazaghi 2023, Sim 2019 and Arman 2024 (BCTQ) show no added benefit over splinting, while Kim 2015 reports benefit over conventional treatment; Lewis 2020 reduced conversion to surgery (59% vs 80%) but tested a bundle. (3) Mabrouk 2026 found desensitization beat neurodynamics, but its effect sizes (d=6.11, d=6.91) are implausibly large and its BCTQ values conflict between table and text, so it does not change this file. (4) Splinting: AAOS 2016 gave a Strong recommendation and the 2019 summary Grade B, while Cochrane 2023 finds insufficient evidence; AAOS 2024 did not carry the 2016 recommendation forward in its summary. (5) Diagnosis: AAOS 2024 favours CTS-6 in lieu of routine testing; Pelosi 2022 says electrodiagnosis should always be done to quantify severity. (6) Keyboard use: AAOS 2024 (workgroup consensus from absence of reliable evidence) reversed the prior moderate association, and Hassan 2022 found HR 0.28 for high computer use from one study with a possibly high-risk reference group, while Coenen 2019 found RR 1.11 for screen work across symptoms that are not CTS-specific. (7) Vibration: Barcenilla 2012, Nilsson 2017 and Palmer 2007 find increased risk; Hassan 2022 does not. (8) Wrist direction: McGorry 2014 found flexion often lowered in vivo pressure, while Keir 1997 and Gelberman 1981 found flexion raised load or pressure. (9) Exercise and nerve size: Altinok 2004 found swelling after provocative exercise in dynamic CTS, while Betancourt 2020 found area fell in larger nerves after circuit training in a different population. (10) Doses: CSP advice conflicts with pressure data on right-angle wrist bends and squeezing. Access. The final JOSPT 2019 and 2026 guidelines were blocked: 2019 grades come from Guideline Central and a draft marked 'Do Not Cite', and 2026 grades come from a commercial third-party summary, so they need checking against the original. AAOS 2024 was read as its published summary, with its 2026 erratum unread. NICE CKS and NG127 and the German AWMF S3 guideline could not be read and are not used. Most new sources are abstract only, and the two Cochrane full texts were read only in part. Indirectness. Pressure studies are mostly in healthy volunteers at low loads, risk data are occupational, and no study found measured push-ups, planks, hangs or barbell grip in CTS. Harms of exercise are essentially unmeasured, not shown to be absent. The only resistance trial found is a single post-release session. Primary doses are from combined-treatment trials or patient information, and the app's adaptations are labelled inference. Red flags on acute CTS, constant numbness and spinal cord signs still rest on an educational summary of AAOS and a small case series: the AAOS summary that was read does not supply them. Not medical advice or treatment.

valuesCorrected: Barcenilla 2012 wrist posture: was given only as not significant; the abstract also reports a significant association under the NIOSH case definition. Added to the rationale and the .md.
Hassan 2022 HR 0.28: reference group corrected from 'high-force' to 'high-risk', the paper's wording.

Zaheer 2023: 'mostly therapist-delivered' corrected, since the full text says a trained physiotherapist applied the techniques in all included studies. No GRADE assessment appears in the full text, not only the abstract.
Jiménez-Del-Barrio 2022: labelled as manual therapy including soft-tissue techniques, not neurodynamic work alone.
Núñez-Cortés 2026: 'one session' corrected to a crossover with one session per condition across 2 visits.
Huang 2024: n=27 kept from the paper's results, with a note that its abstract says 29 recruited.
Keir and Bach 2000: flexor entry into the tunnel labelled as calculated, not measured.
Page 2012 RR 1.26 (.md): outcome corrected from general improvement to normal sensory latency, in a trial that also used activity modification.
Sim 2019 (.md): 0.53 and 0.48 labelled as within-group changes.
Li and Jordan 2026 (.md): added that baseline pressure was set near 30 mmHg.
Links: 13 europepmc.org/article URLs returned HTTP 403 when fetched, so their JSON url now points to the matching PubMed record.
PMCIDs added from PubMed: bartkowiak_2019, kozak_2015, christodoulou_2025.
Access labels: all 14 not_reconfirmed entries replaced with what was actually read in this check.
Sadler 2025 (.md): link changed to the AAFP page given in the JSON.
unverifiable: JOSPT 2019 and 2026 final guidelines: only PubMed records, Guideline Central, Physiotutors and the 'Do Not Cite' draft could be read. The grades are second-hand.
AAOS/ASSH 2024: only the published summary was read, and only the title of its 2026 erratum (PMID 42825588), which has no abstract. The erratum's content could change a statement here.
iatroX red flag wording: iatroX tags it to AAOS, but it does not appear in the AAOS summary read, so it could not be traced to the original.
Abstract-only sources were checked against the abstract alone; their methods and tables were not read.
Sadler 2025: free excerpt only, and PubMed has no abstract.
catalog:wrist-extension match and the stop-exercise wording in some red flags are app decisions, not source claims, so they could not be confirmed from any paper.
